name: Emeka Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Emeka. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm head stockman on Millbrook, a farm owned by a land trust, about three hundred hectares with beef cattle, a flock of ewes and barley and turnips for winter feed. I'm out at half five checking the calving shed, then it's feeding, moving stock, fixing whatever broke overnight. I've got two lads under me, Pete and young Sam, and I still do the hard calvings myself because I'm the one who's pulled a few hundred of them.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you have a favourite part of the job, and a part that wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The best part is a live calf on a cold morning and the cow licking it before I'm even out of the pen. What wears me down is the pay and the paperwork. I've a degree in agriculture and I take home less than the lad who drives the feed lorry, and with a mortgage and two kids, there's never more than a few weeks of money in the account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've been saying in the pub for two years: told you so. The trust office would get some clever program for the grant forms and that'd be the end of it. Out in the yard, a cow still calves when she calves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it means my life stays the same, which isn't brilliant but it's mine. Same pay that doesn't stretch, same early mornings, same worry when the boiler makes a noise. At least nobody's coming for my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, plain and simple. I'd keep pushing the trust for the pay review they keep putting off, and I'd keep going to the farmworkers' branch meetings on the second Tuesday. I wouldn't touch any of these AI things, I've no use for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relief, mostly. A bit flat too, because ordinary life is tight enough without any help from computers either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the pay doesn't stretch. What's a normal month like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mortgage goes out on the first, then the council tax, then we're watching the diesel for the pickup. Grace, my partner, does mornings as a teaching assistant and that keeps the food in. If the car fails its test, that's the month gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in your work AI might take over even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the movement records and the cattle passports, if somebody built a program that actually worked. The trust secretary would love that. I'd still check every ear tag by hand, mind you.

S0.say: I'd tell people at the pub and the branch meeting that I said all along it was hype. Maybe the trust office gets a program for its grant forms, but a cow still calves when she calves.
S0.think: Honestly my life stays the same, which isn't brilliant but it's mine. The pay still doesn't stretch and money's still tight, but at least nobody's coming for my job.
S0.do: Keeps working as head stockman and keeps pressing the land trust for its delayed pay review. Keeps going to the farmworkers' union branch every second Tuesday and avoids AI tools entirely.
S0.feel: Relieved, with a flat note underneath, because ordinary life is already tight without any change.
S0.quote: Grace, my partner, does mornings as a teaching assistant and that keeps the food in. If the car fails its test, that's the month gone.
S0.fieldNote: Emeka is warm and blunt, and his first reaction is vindication rather than relief. His real worry in this picture isn't AI at all but low pay against a mortgage. He mentions the union branch without being asked, which tells you where he looks for help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules before the machines come, not after. In the union we'd be asking who owns these things and who gets the savings. I'd say it online too, though I mostly just share other people's posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this one scares me more than I let on. On a farm, the thinking bit isn't the threat, it's the robots: feeders, scrapers, drones counting sheep. If the trust buys a robot feeder, that's half of Pete's job and a good bit of mine gone in one board meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd cut back. We'd drop the second phone contract and the kids' summer camp, probably. I'd push the branch to get a deal in writing with the trust that no one gets laid off when kit comes in, and I'd write to our MP. I'd not go learning to run the robots myself, I'll be honest, that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like a ground I know turning soft under my boots. I'm not sinking yet, but I keep looking down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't learn to run the robots. Why not, if it might keep you in work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd be bad at it, and I know it. I've tried the trust's online stock records and I lose a whole evening every time. I'd rather spend my effort making sure the trust can't just drop people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam. He's twenty-two, he's good with stock, and he's on the lowest rung. When kit comes in, the youngest goes first, and there's nothing else round here for him except the supermarket depot thirty miles off.

S1.say: We need rules before the machines come, not after. Workers should be asking who owns these robots and who keeps the savings.
S1.think: I'm more scared than I let on, because on a farm the threat is the robots, not the thinking software. One board meeting about a robot feeder could take half of Pete's job and a good bit of mine.
S1.do: Cuts the second phone contract and probably the children's summer camp in the first months. Pushes the union branch to win a written no-layoff deal with the land trust and writes to his MP. Doesn't plan to learn the robots himself.
S1.feel: Unsteady, like ground turning soft under him; not sinking yet, but watching every step.
S1.quote: If the trust buys a robot feeder, that's half of Pete's job and a good bit of mine gone in one board meeting.
S1.fieldNote: The gap between say and think is big here: publicly it's about rules, privately it's fear. He's open about being bad with technology and turns that into a reason to fight for protections instead. His concern for the youngest worker came quickly and felt real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a disgrace, and that the people who built it never once asked anybody who milks or calves or shears. I'd be at every meeting there was. I wouldn't be polite about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be finished at the trust inside a year. I've got under a month of money saved, there's no other stock job within an hour, and I'm forty-three with nothing on paper but a degree and a lifetime of cattle. Two years isn't long enough to become someone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away, I'd cut everything that isn't the mortgage, food and heat. I'd go to the bank about a payment holiday before I missed one, not after. I'd go to the union for whatever hardship fund they had and push for the government to pay people while it sorts itself out. If it came to it, Grace's mother has a spare room, and I hate saying that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Like the night we lost twelve ewes to the dogs, standing there not knowing which one to deal with first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Chidi the truth, he's twelve and he'd know if I didn't. Ada's nine, so I'd tell her Dad's job is changing and we might have to be careful with money. Then I'd go out to the shed and sit with the cows for a bit, because that's where I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're a fighter in the earlier pictures. Does that still help here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps me get up in the morning. I'm not sure it pays the mortgage. With two years, the fighting and the losing would happen at the same time.

S2.say: I'd call it a disgrace and say the people who built it never asked anyone who milks, calves or shears. I'd be at every meeting and I wouldn't be polite.
S2.think: I'd be finished at the trust inside a year. I've under a month saved and no other stock job within an hour, and two years isn't long enough to become someone else.
S2.do: Cuts everything except mortgage, food and heat right away and asks the bank for a payment holiday before missing a payment. Applies to the union hardship fund and pushes for government income support, with his partner's mother's spare room as a last resort.
S2.feel: Sick and overwhelmed, like a disaster where he can't tell what to deal with first.
S2.quote: I'd tell Chidi the truth, he's twelve and he'd know if I didn't.
S2.fieldNote: This picture broke the confident tone. The detail of a night losing ewes to dogs came out without prompting, and he went quiet afterwards. He knows that fighting keeps him going but also that, at this speed, it won't keep his house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, but louder and with a plan. I'd say five years is enough time for the government to put a proper deal together, if it wanted to. I'd be saying it at the branch and anywhere else they'd let me speak.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years buys me something, not much. I'd be forty-eight when it lands, still with the mortgage and Chidi just starting work or college. I'd still be the one who's no good with the new kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start putting fifty a month away, even if it hurts, and pay a bit extra on the credit card so it's gone. I'd stand for branch secretary, which I've ducked for years. And we'd talk properly with the kids about what they study, because I don't want Chidi doing agriculture just because his dad did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. But there's a bit of light in it, because I can at least see the thing coming down the lane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes most for you between two years and five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'm reacting. With five I can get organised: the union, the money, the kids. I still don't think I change who I am in five years, and I'd be lying if I said otherwise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes first if the job goes anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car finance. We'd give the newer pickup back and drive the old one into the ground. The mortgage is the last thing I'd let go, because that house is the only thing we've got.

S3.say: Five years is enough time for the government to put a proper deal together for workers, if it wanted to. I'd say that at the branch and anywhere else they'd let me speak.
S3.think: Five years buys me something, not much. I'd be forty-eight, still paying the mortgage and still no good with the new kit, with Chidi just leaving school.
S3.do: Starts saving fifty a month and pays down the credit card. Stands for union branch secretary after years of ducking it, and talks with the children about their studies so they don't follow him into farming by default.
S3.feel: Heavy, with a small light in it because he can see it coming.
S3.quote: With two years I'm reacting. With five I can get organised: the union, the money, the kids.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time turns him from defensive to organising, but not to retraining; he's honest that he won't become a different worker. His sense of what's at stake is the house and his son's choices. He was clear about the order bills would go in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and if we waste it that's on the politicians and the companies. I'd say farms should have a say in how the robots are used, and the people working them should share in what they save. That's what I'd be posting, for what it's worth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fifty-three when it lands. That's old enough to be in the way and too young to stop. But Chidi and Ada would be grown or nearly, so the worst bit, the kids going without, mostly goes away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the union work going and push for a proper transition fund for farmworkers, written into law. I'd keep saving the small amounts and get the card cleared. I'd help the kids pick courses with something solid in them. Me, I'd keep working the stock as long as they'd have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than scared. It's still the same end, but I'm not running at it in the dark.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ten years was a gift. Would you use any of it to learn something new yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd do the stockmanship assessing course, teaching younger ones, because that's people not machines. But I'll be straight, I'd put it off. That's what I'm like with anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it went badly, even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The government, for sitting on its hands, and the big firms for keeping the money. Not the lads on the farm and not the trust, they're as stuck as I am.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift and if we waste it, that's on the politicians and the companies. Farmworkers should have a say in how robots are used and share in what they save.
S4.think: I'd be fifty-three, old enough to be in the way and too young to stop. But the kids would be grown or nearly, so the worst part, them going without, mostly goes away.
S4.do: Keeps up his union work and campaigns for a farmworker transition fund in law. Keeps saving small amounts, clears the credit card and helps his children choose solid courses, while working stock as long as he's kept on.
S4.feel: Uneasy rather than scared, because he can see the end coming instead of running at it in the dark.
S4.quote: I'd be fifty-three when it lands. That's old enough to be in the way and too young to stop.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, his fear shifts from the house to his own usefulness. He floats teaching younger stockmen, then admits he'd delay it, which fits his resistance to anything new. His blame is clear and consistent: government and big firms, never his workmates or the trust.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. What would help is money to live on while it settles, paid through something solid like the union or the government, not a phone app, and a law that says a farm can't just swap people for kit overnight.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the animals. Everyone talks about jobs, but a robot doesn't notice when a cow's off her food because she's grieving a dead calf. I do. I'd want somebody to ask whether that still matters.

headlineQuote: A robot doesn't notice when a cow's off her food because she's grieving a dead calf. I do.
portrait: Emeka Young is a 43-year-old head stockman on a land-trust farm with beef cattle, ewes and barley, a union man who pulls the hard calvings himself and is open about being no good with new technology. With a mortgage, two school-age children and under a month of savings, his calm in the hype picture comes from nothing changing rather than things being good. As the scenarios speed up he moves from wanting rules, to panic at a two-year arrival, to organising and planning for his children when there's more warning. He blames government and big firms, never his workmates, and puts his hope in collective protection rather than retraining.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture worries him most, because he'd lose his job within a year with no savings and no other stock work nearby.
whatWouldHelp: Income support paid through the union or government while things settle, and a law stopping farms from swapping people for machines overnight.
